extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, and designers of ornamentation (especially those working in Gothic/Christian/romanesque traditions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and evaluating ornament on architectural features (tympanum, gable, shaft, cornice, capital), emphasizing proportion, profile curvature, ornament placement, and workmanship in Gothic/Christian and related traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tympanum treatment and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The tympanum... is almost always charged with a series of rich figure sculptures, solemn in feeling and consecutive in subject. It occupies in Christian sacred edifices very nearly the position of the pediment in Greek sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the tympanum in a conspicuous position near the eye and above the entrance; charge it with rich, solemn, and thematically consecutive figure sculpture (akin to the narrative program of a Greek pediment). Avoid trivial or decorative-only treatment that neglects solemnity and narrative sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gable apex treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief difficulty in treating a gable lies in the excessive sharpness of its upper point... the most beautiful victory I have ever seen obtained over this difficulty was by placing a sharp shield... at the apex of the gable, which exactly reversed the offensive lines, yet without actually breaking them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate the harshness of a gable's apex by concealing or reversing the inside meeting lines—use finials, shields, or similar devices that preserve continuity while softening conspicuous sharp joins. Examples: porches of Abbeville, tombs of Verona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shaft: primary beauty is proportion and expression of strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Now the principal beauty of a shaft is its perfect proportion to its work, — its exact expression of necessary strength. If this has been truly attained, it will hardly need, in some cases hardly bear, more decoration than is given to it by its own rounding and taper curvatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize correct proportions and the shaft's inherent curvature over applied ornament. If the shaft already expresses necessary strength, avoid added carving that weakens (intaglio) or overcharges (relief) its visual and structural clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intaglio and excessive relief on shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: if we cut ornaments in intaglio on its surface, we weaken it; if we leave them in relief, we overcharge it...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use deep incisions (intaglio) that compromise perceived solidity; avoid heavy relief that breaks the shaft's sweep. Ornament must not break the contour or suggest structural weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale-appropriate ornamentation (colossal vs diminutive vs middle)
rubrics_metrics.description: decorations are admissible on colossal and on diminutive shafts, which are wrong upon those of middle size... the mean standard would be of some twenty feet in height, by eight or nine in circumference: then this will be the size on which decoration is most difficult and dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt ornament to shaft scale: colossal shafts can bear incisions/sculpture if legible at distance; very small shafts may be lavishly ornamented so long as the form remains clear; avoid heavy ornament on medium-sized shafts (~mean standard) where it becomes injurious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility of design at intended viewing distance
rubrics_metrics.description: one of their chief merits, as examples of method, being the perfect decision and visibility of their designs at the necessary distance: contrast with these the incrustations of bas-relief on the Trajan pillar, much interfering with the smooth lines of the shaft, and yet themselves untraceable, if not invisible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure ornament and incision are decisive and visible at the distance from which they will be read; fine bas-relief that becomes untraceable at viewing distance is unsuitable for shafts and large members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate fluting for middle-sized shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: On shafts of middle size, the only ornament which has ever been accepted as right, is the Doric fluting... The Corinthian fluting... destroyed the serenity of the shaft altogether, and is always rigid and meagre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For middle-sized shafts, prefer Doric fluting (succession of unequal lines of shade) sparingly; avoid Corinthian-style deep multiplication or square-ridged fluting that rigidifies and weakens the shaft's serenity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve shaft form visibility on small shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: on shafts of inferior size, every species of decoration may be wisely lavished, and in any quantity, so only that the form of the shaft be clearly visible... barbarism begins wherever the sculpture is either so bossy, or so deeply cut, as to break the contour of the shaft, or compromise its solidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When richly decorating small shafts, ensure ornamentation does not obscure the shaft's outline or give a shapeless mass; inlaid patterns that preserve contour may add preciousness without compromising function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiral/twisted shaft composition
rubrics_metrics.description: it has been spoken against... that no twisted shaft shall be single, but composed of at least two distinct members, twined with each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid single twisted shafts; compose twisted shafts of two or more distinct members twined together, keeping spirals slight and pure (as in Romanesque), not exaggerated (as in bad Renaissance examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use nature and grouped forms as models
rubrics_metrics.description: Many forest trees present, in their accidental contortions, types of most complicated spiral shafts, the plan being originally of a grouped shaft rising from several roots... the reader will never find models for every kind of shaft decoration... as he will find in the great forest aisle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study natural grouped forms (tree stems, roots, boughs) as models for shaft grouping, spiral treatment, and surface ornament; natural forms often yield more graceful and varied types than forced invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cornice and capital families: concave vs convex profiles
rubrics_metrics.description: That both the cornice and capital are, with reference to the slope of their profile or bell, to be divided into two great orders; in one of which the ornament is convex, and in the other concave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the two primal families (concave and convex) when selecting cornice/capital profiles; choose profile according to the architectural role and expression required (supporting vs crowning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four central cornice profile types (a, b, c, d) as roots
rubrics_metrics.description: These four profiles will represent all the simple cornices in the world; represent them, I mean, as central types... a and b (concave family), c and d (convex family).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the four central profile types as root-templates; adapt slope and curve from natural lines (e.g., salvia leaf) rather than defaulting to circular segments; variation arises from slope and curve choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for pure and graceful curvature where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: None of the types are, however, found in perfection of curvature, except in the best work... a is the most graceful of all simple profiles of cornice and capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for pure curvature in profiles (where feasible); while circular segments may be used for noble, massive effect, finer curvature yields a more graceful capital/cornice in the best work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ogee/combined group and three-curve profiles
rubrics_metrics.description: we have next to note the combined group, formed by the concave and convex lines joined... applying the Matterhorn curve... types e,f,g,h... another limb is added... composed of three curves of unequal lengths and different arrangements (k–p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ogee and multi-curve profiles (three-curve arrangements) to achieve richer cornice types; prefer the arrangements noted as most beautiful (e.g., Matterhorn lines m and n) and avoid overcomplicating with many small added curves unless appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit unnecessary profile complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: If we were to add a fourth curve to the component series, we should have forty-eight more cornices: but there is no use in pursuing the system further, as such arrangements are very rare and easily resolved into the simpler types with certain arbitrary additions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous multiplication of component curves; prefer simpler central types with carefully-placed additions rather than excessive fragmentation of the profile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must be rooted and express upward spring
rubrics_metrics.description: they all, except b, are distinctly rooted in the lower part of the cornice, and spring to the top. This arrangement is constant in all the best cornices and capitals; and it is essential to the expression of the supporting power of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design cornice and capital ornament to root visibly at the lower part and spring upward — this vertical, ascendant arrangement expresses support. Avoid 'running' ornaments that flow horizontally or twine round features meant to express support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running/banded ornament is improper for support features
rubrics_metrics.description: It is exactly opposed to the system of running cornices and banded capitals, in which the ornament flows along them horizontally, or is twined round them... Such cornices have arisen from a mistaken appliance of the running ornaments... A tendril may nobly follow the outline of an arch, but must not creep along a cornice, nor swathe or bandage a capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply archivolt/jamb running ornament or twining tendrils to cornices and capitals that have definite functions of support; such placement weakens the expression of rooted strength and is indicative of declining style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible exceptions: heavy/firm running ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: some of the Italian cornices which are actually composed by running tendrils... are so massive in their treatment, and so marked and firm in their vertical and arched lines, that they are nearly as suggestive of support as if they had been arranged on the rooted system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Running or banded ornament may be acceptable only when its massing and vertical/arched emphasis still convey support (as in certain Italian examples); use caution and ensure the overall effect does not read as swathed or bandaged confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy, naturalism, and suggestiveness over conventional repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: there are two great new elements visible — energy and naturalism... those Christian cornices are, as far as may be, suggestive... with the fewest possible incisions, and those of the easiest shape, they suggest the true image, of clusters of leaves... The Greek egg and arrow cornice is a nonsense cornice... conventionalised into a monotonous successiveness of nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor designs that show energetic workmanship and naturalistic suggestion (leaf clusters, rooted forms) with minimal, well-placed incisions. Avoid conventional, repetitive patterns (egg-and-arrow, stylized arrows/eggs) that are decoratively pleasant but meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of cutting: precision, sharpness, and truthful workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: His work is absolutely unreprovable; keen, and true, as Nature's own; his entire force is in it, and fixed on seeing that every line of it shall be sharp and right: the faithful energy is in him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure chiselling is energetic, precise, and true — lines must be sharp and correct. Avoid dulness, blunted edges, or meandering inlay that signals lack of craftsmanship and weakens design integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive natural modelling in ornament (e.g., leaf curling)
rubrics_metrics.description: flowers have been added between the clusters of leaves, and the leaves themselves curled over: observe the well-directed thought of the sculptor in this curling; — the old incisions are retained below... but those incisions now stand for the under surface of the leaf; and behold, when it turns over, on the top of it you see true ribs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design ornament with coherent natural modelling: use incisions to indicate under-surfaces and add top ribs where forms turn over, creating believable foliage that reads correctly in light and shadow.
